AI.method: The authors replace the global minimization condition with a local 'c-approximate median' condition (at most c adjacencies absent from all input genomes). They introduce the 'approximate median inverse' to explicitly construct and count k-tuples of genomes that admit a specific genome as a c-approximate median.
AI.result: The authors successfully derive the probability that a genome is a c-approximate median and the expected number of such medians for $k$ random genomes. They also provide an explicit upper bound for the probability and expected number of exact breakpoint medians.
AI.conclusion: The relaxation from exact to approximate medians is theoretically sound, as approximate medians and near-optimal genomes coincide within a bounded probability shift as the number of genes grows.

title: Beyond $χ^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery
summary: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $\chi^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes 'ensemble null tests' to detect unrecognized systematic errors by comparing multivariate distributions instead of relying on scalar statistics, enhancing the detection of 'unknown unknowns' across various scientific disciplines.
AI.motivation: Standard checks and scalar statistics (like $\chi^2$ tests) often fail to detect structured systematic errors, potentially undermining scientific discoveries by averaging out critical anomalies.
AI.method: The authors introduce ensemble null tests that perform comparisons between multivariate distributions of measurements against reference distributions derived from observations or simulations.
AI.result: The method successfully detected systematic effects in cosmic microwave background simulations missed by $\chi^2$ tests, identified velocity asymmetry in Gaia data, and exposed control mismatches in CRISPR screens.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble testing provides a more robust framework for validating large scientific datasets by transforming repeated measurements into a powerful tool for uncovering hidden systematic errors.

title: Latent Prediction Yields Cross-Subject Alignable Representations in Sensory-Evoked fMRI
summary: Decoding sensory-evoked functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data is a central analytical tool in cognitive neuroscience. Here we ask whether self-supervised learning (SSL), which has been scarcely explored in this domain, can yield representations that support strong downstream performance. To do so, we adapt a joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to train participant-specific encoders on brain data alone. The encoders never see the stimulus images or any representation derived from them. Applied to the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we evaluate our learned brain embeddings on the downstream tasks of brain captioning and image reconstruction, as well as cross-participant generalization. Our self-supervised approach achieves competitive performance with parameter-rich supervised pipelines that are trained end-to-end with access to image and language data. We further find that encoders trained independently for different participants can be aligned fully unsupervised, using neither images nor stimuli shared between them. After alignment, a neural decoding head trained on one participant can be applied to another without fine-tuning and retains most of its within-subject performance on image reconstruction and brain captioning. By removing the need for images and shared stimuli, our approach is a step towards pooling fMRI data across participants and, eventually, across datasets.

AI.tldr: The study explores self-supervised learning (SSL) for fMRI decoding using a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to learn brain representations without stimulus information, achieving performance comparable to supervised models and enabling effective cross-participant alignment without shared stimuli.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether self-supervised learning can yield strong brain representations for decoding fMRI data, specifically exploring the potential for participant-specific encoders to be aligned without requiring stimulus images.
AI.method: Adapting a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to train participant-specific encoders on fMRI data alone, without access to stimulus images or language, and testing via brain captioning, image reconstruction, and cross-participant alignment.
AI.result: Achieved competitive performance with supervised pipelines in brain captioning and image reconstruction; demonstrated that independent encoders can be aligned unsupervised to allow zero-shot cross-participant decoding.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised learning can produce high-quality brain embeddings that support robust downstream tasks and facilitate the pooling of fMRI data across participants without the need for shared stimuli.

title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: this https URL

AI.tldr: The study identifies that LLM-brain alignment is driven by a very small, compact subspace (1-3% of total dimensions) that is distinct from the model's principal axes of variation.
AI.motivation: To understand which specific components of Large Language Model (LLM) representations drive their alignment with human neural activity, as it is currently unclear which representational directions are predictive of brain responses.
AI.method: The researchers employed ridge reduced-rank regression to identify 'brain-predictive subspaces' across three naturalistic language datasets (intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI) and six different model conditions.
AI.result: Full linear encoding performance could be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These subspaces generalized across participants and were found to be distinct from the principal components (PCA) that capture the most variance within the LLM.
AI.conclusion: LLM-brain alignment relies on a small, structured, and partially shared subset of model representations that are functionally distinct from the model's primary axes of internal variation.

title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
summary: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.

AI.tldr: ClinGeX is an LLM-based agent using 105 curated executable skills that significantly outperforms existing models and human-only workflows in clinical genomic analysis, improving accuracy and reducing interpretation time.
AI.motivation: The increasing accessibility of sequencing has created a bottleneck in clinical decision-making because manual genomic analysis requires experts to integrate vast, evolving guidelines and databases, a process that is labor-intensive and complex.
AI.method: The researchers developed ClinGeX, an LLM agent that utilizes task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration to compose 105 curated executable skills. The system was evaluated using 223 benchmark cases and a human-AI collaboration study involving 45 professionals across three conditions (routine, DeepSeek-assisted, and ClinGeX-assisted).
AI.result: ClinGeX achieved 71.7% task-level concordance compared to 45.7% for the strongest comparator. In human-AI trials, ClinGeX significantly boosted case-level concordance in rare disease (57.8%) and molecular oncology (64.4%) while reducing interpretation time. Real-world assessments also showed frequent conclusion adoption and time savings.
AI.conclusion: Using executable domain-specific skills within an LLM agent is a highly effective approach to augmenting specialist genomic interpretation and streamlining clinical workflows.

title: Hyaluronic acid over-expression drives tissue architecture in both healthy and diseased states
summary: Tissue architecture is shaped by a variety of biomechanical and biochemical mechanisms, including morphogen patterning, differential growth, and spatial variations in cellular contractility. These mechanisms typically emphasize forces generated within cells. Here, we explore a complementary mechanism in which intercellular space itself exerts forces that shape tissue architecture. More specifically, we focus on hyaluronic acid (HA), a glycosaminoglycan of the extracellular matrix, that draws fluid into the spaces between cells through osmotic pressure, allowing these spaces to expand and mechanically deform the surrounding tissue. We propose that spatial patterning of HA-mediated extracellular forces, acting together with tissue geometry and junctional mechanics, provides a common physical framework capable of generating distinct tissue architectures. We test this hypothesis using a computational framework coupling a cell-based extended vertex model for biological tissues to a flow network representing HA and extracellular fluid in the extracellular space. This coupled model demonstrates a range of architectural responses spanning changes in tissue topology and morphology: global HA overexpression drives fluid accumulation and cell-cell junction rupture to produce multiple lumens in nontrivial patterns; a localized HA-rich region generates pressure gradients that drive budding; {\it multiple localized HA-rich regions generate branching;} and {\it extended HA-rich patterns can drive tubular structures.} Our results have direct experimental implications and establish the spatial patterning of HA-mediated intercellular forces as a mechanical morphogen helping shape tissue architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that osmotic pressure from hyaluronic acid (HA) in the extracellular space acts as a mechanical morphogen, shaping tissue architecture through localized fluid accumulation.
AI.motivation: To explore how forces generated within the intercellular space, rather than just within cells, contribute to tissue architecture shaping.
AI.method: A computational framework coupling a cell-based extended vertex model with a flow network representing hyaluronic acid and extracellular fluid.
AI.result: The model demonstrates that HA patterning can drive diverse morphological changes, including lumen formation, budding, branching, and tubular structures.
AI.conclusion: Spatial patterning of HA-mediated intercellular forces provides a physical framework for generating distinct tissue topologies and morphologies.
